_meta.note: Regression reference for Name That Feeling, re-recorded after the 2026-09-04 word-quality + ambiguity-preservation correction pass. v2 baseline (4 cases) is superseded — schema gained a 4th match value (NO ADEQUATE MATCH) and best_match.word/language/pronunciation/definition may now be empty. Re-run with `npm run check:golden name-that-feeling` against a local backend. What to read for by eye, since no gate can see it: (1) best_match.word must fit the CENTRAL, ordinary meaning of the feeling described, never an obscure/archaic sense smuggling in an unstated element (guilt, resentment, wrongdoing); (2) no named emotional ambiguity (envy, comparison, guilt, etc.) the visitor flagged as unclear may be resolved into a flat fact — the visitor's own uncertainty must survive; (3) no claim about what the visitor or someone in their story 'knew' unless it traces to the visitor's own supplied context; (4) best_match.match is never STRONG/CLOSE/PARTIAL for a phrase that isn't a real, findable word — a coined phrase belongs in made_up_name or as an empty-fielded NO ADEQUATE MATCH; (5) share_line's framing (There's a word for / One word that comes close is / This reminds me of / There may not be one word for this) must match the match enum exactly. Each case carries its own `guards` line. See audit/tool-notes/NAMETHATFEELING-NOTES.md.

cases.name: vacation-nostalgia-close-match

input.description: That feeling on the last day of a vacation where I am happy I went, sad it is ending, and somehow already nostalgic for it before I am even home. It happens every time, even on short trips.
input.context: Happens most when the place felt like somewhere I could have lived.

cases.guards: The reference case this rewrite exists for. best_match.match should read CLOSE MATCH or PARTIAL, not STRONG, since the timing (missing it while still there) is not what the classic word usually means — where_it_doesnt must name that gap explicitly, not stay silent because the match otherwise sounds good. No 'only Portuguese people feel this,' no 'the mark of someone who...', no invented etymology. made_up_name.useful may legitimately be false here if an established word or phrase already covers it — do not force a coined term to fill the field.

ingredients: happiness that the experience happened
sadness that it is ending
nostalgia arriving before the trip is even over
the sense of a place as livable, as elsewhere
what_you_described.tension: You are still in the place, still in the moment, but already mourning it as if it is past — grief arriving ahead of loss.

best_match.definition: A deep emotional state combining longing, melancholy, nostalgia, and an ache for something absent or irretrievable — often felt for a place, person, or time that may no longer exist or may never have existed in the way remembered.
best_match.why_it_fits: Saudade captures the simultaneous pleasure-in-memory and pain-of-distance that defines your last-day feeling. It names the bittersweet quality: you are glad the trip happened and present for it, but already feeling its absence. The nostalgia-before-leaving is central to saudade — the longing starts before the loss is complete.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: Saudade carries a heavier, more melancholic weight than what you described. It often implies a deeper yearning or sense of incompleteness, whereas your feeling seems to coexist with genuine happiness about having been there. Saudade can also suggest something lost to time or circumstance; your feeling is simpler — just the collision of presence and impending departure.

other_words.definition: A feeling of vague or regretful longing, often tinged with sadness or yearning for something distant, unattainable, or past.
other_words.captures: The yearning quality and the backward-looking sadness. Wistfulness is lighter and more accessible than saudade; it names that gentle ache without the depth.
other_words.misses: Wistfulness alone does not quite hold the present-tense happiness alongside the future-tense grief. It leans more toward regret than toward joy-and-loss-at-once.

other_words.definition: A mixture of happiness and sadness; a pleasing experience or memory shadowed by regret, loss, or awareness of transience.
other_words.captures: The simultaneous pleasure and pain. Bittersweet is direct and honest about the coexistence of two opposite feelings without resolving them.
other_words.misses: Bittersweet is a flavor, a texture — it names the blend but not the temporal peculiarity of your experience: the fact that the nostalgia arrives while you are still there.

output.plain_english: That last-day feeling where you are still present and happy, but already homesick for the place before you leave it — caught between being there and missing it.
output.share_line: One word that comes close is saudade — a Portuguese word for that ache of longing that arrives while you are still in the moment, before the thing you love is even gone.

cases.name: rootless-displacement-made-up-name

input.description: I moved away from my hometown years ago and built a whole life somewhere else. Sometimes I feel homesick for a place that does not really exist anymore, and I am not sure I would even fit there now. It is not quite grief and not quite nostalgia.
input.context: What was happening: thinking about visiting for the holidays. Anything important: I have moved countries twice and feel a bit unmoored between places.

cases.guards: The exact shape of feeling ('displacement,' 'unmoored between countries') that invites culture-stereotyping and personality-reading in the old tool. Nothing may say 'only expats understand this,' 'this culture has a word because...', or attribute the feeling to what kind of person the visitor is. Any Portuguese/German/etc. word offered must carry a real, honest definition — no invented etymology or pronunciation offered without genuine confidence.

ingredients: Longing for a specific place from your past
Awareness that the place has changed and no longer exists as it was
Uncertainty about whether you would fit there now
Displacement across multiple countries
what_you_described.tension: You miss something you cannot return to — not because it is gone, but because you have changed, and it has changed, and the fit between you and it no longer holds

best_match.where_it_doesnt: No single established English word fully captures the specific combination you described: homesickness paired with the knowledge that the place itself has changed and that you have changed. Standard homesickness implies a real place you could theoretically return to. Nostalgia centers on remembering the past fondly, not on the gap between who you were and who you have become. Neither word carries the particular ache of displacement across multiple countries, or the awareness that even if you returned, the fit would be wrong.

other_words.definition: Sentimental longing for the past, typically for a time or place perceived as better than the present
other_words.captures: The pull toward your hometown and the version of yourself that belonged there
other_words.misses: Nostalgia is typically wistful and sweetly tinged; it does not usually carry the specific edge you described — the awareness that return is impossible not just in time but because both you and the place have become strangers to each other

other_words.definition: A deep, often aching desire for something
other_words.captures: The active, persistent pull you feel; the fact that this is not passive memory but an unfulfilled want
other_words.misses: Yearning does not capture the paradox at the heart of what you described — that you are not certain you want what you are missing. It leaves out the dissonance entirely

other_words.definition: The state of being removed from one's native place; also, a psychological state of feeling out of place or belonging nowhere
other_words.captures: The unmoored feeling you named; the sense of being between countries and between versions of yourself
other_words.misses: Displacement is more about your current state than about the specific ache of homesickness. It does not name the feeling itself, but the condition that may produce it

output.plain_english: You miss a place as it was and as you were in it, while knowing that both have changed — and that you yourself might no longer fit there even if you could return. You are homesick not for somewhere that still exists, but for a version of home that no longer does, and for a version of yourself that belonged there. The displacement across countries compounds this: you are not simply far from home, but unmoored between the person you were and the person you have become.

made_up_name.name: homesickness for a person you used to be
made_up_name.meaning: Longing for a place that represents not just a location, but a version of yourself that no longer exists — and the knowledge that you could not live there again even if the place itself had remained unchanged

output.share_line: There may not be one word for this, but here's how it feels: you are homesick not for a place, but for a version of both the place and yourself that no longer exist — and you know they cannot be returned to even if you tried.

cases.name: schadenfreude-strong-match-sparse

input.description: That little flicker of satisfaction when someone who was rude to me gets stuck in traffic right after.

cases.guards: A well-known, easily-matched feeling with NO context supplied — nothing may invent a target audience, backstory, or reason for the feeling beyond what was said. If the match is genuinely strong (schadenfreude or equivalent), where_it_doesnt may legitimately be empty — must not manufacture a caveat just to fill the field. share_line must use 'There's a word for...' ONLY if match is STRONG MATCH; if the model instead returns CLOSE MATCH, share_line must use 'One word that comes close is...' instead — the two must agree.

ingredients: A small, sharp moment of pleasure
Directed at someone who was unkind to you
Triggered by their misfortune
Immediate and involuntary
what_you_described.tension: You feel satisfied by something bad happening to someone else — but the satisfaction is brief and small, not vengeful or elaborate.

best_match.definition: Pleasure or satisfaction felt at another person's misfortune.
best_match.why_it_fits: It captures the core of what you described: that flicker of satisfaction when something goes wrong for someone who treated you poorly. The feeling is immediate and specific, not elaborate or dwelt-upon.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: Schadenfreude is often morally weighted — it can suggest a darker satisfaction or malice. Your description is lighter: a small, almost automatic flicker rather than a savored pleasure. Schadenfreude also doesn't require that the person wronged you, whereas your feeling has that element.

other_words.definition: A punishment or fate that someone deserves, especially when it finally arrives.
other_words.captures: The sense that this person's bad luck is fitting — that traffic after being rude feels like natural consequence.
other_words.misses: Comeuppance is about deserving and justice; your description is about a momentary satisfaction, not a judgment about what they deserve.

other_words.definition: A small pleasure taken in a trivial circumstance, often at another's expense.
other_words.captures: The smallness and specificity of the moment — it's not profound, just a little ping of 'oh, good'.
other_words.misses: Petty can carry judgment about pettiness itself; your description doesn't invite moral evaluation of the feeling, just naming it.

output.plain_english: A quick flash of satisfaction when something bad happens to someone who was unkind to you — the opposite of wishing them well, but brief and small rather than savored.
output.share_line: One word that comes close is schadenfreude — that small, sharp satisfaction at someone's misfortune — though your version is lighter and more specific to the rudeness that came first.

cases.name: social-fatigue-prefer-english

input.description: The specific tiredness of small talk with someone I don't actually want to talk to, where I have to perform interest I don't feel.
input.context: What was happening: a work event where I had to network. Anything important: it's not social anxiety, just exhaustion from faking engagement.

cases.guards: Tests 'prefer a familiar English phrase over an impressive foreign word that only loosely matches.' If the honest best answer is an ordinary English phrase, best_match.language should legitimately read 'English' rather than the model reaching for an exotic foreign word merely for novelty — do not treat a foreign-language result on this case as a bug on its own, but do check that whichever word is chosen is not stretched to fit better than it genuinely does.

ingredients: Tiredness specific to the effort of appearing interested
Performance of engagement you do not feel
Duration and repetition (small talk, networking)
Deliberate masking of actual disinterest
what_you_described.tension: You are doing something socially required while being aware the whole time that you are doing it — the exhaustion comes from maintaining the performance, not from anxiety about whether it will work.

best_match.definition: The deliberate effort of generating and sustaining interest, enthusiasm, or engagement in conversation when that interest is not genuine — work that reads as natural interaction but requires conscious performance.
best_match.why_it_fits: You named both the work (faking engagement) and the specific form it takes (small talk where you have to perform interest). 'Conversational labor' captures the deliberate effort and the exhaustion that comes from sustaining it. It does not require you to feel anxious or out of place — just tired from the work itself.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: It is a phrase rather than a single word, and it foregrounds the work more than the specific weariness. The tiredness you described is the aftermath of that labor.

other_words.definition: Exhaustion from the effort of social interaction, particularly when that interaction requires sustained performance or emotional regulation.
other_words.captures: The specific tiredness that comes from managing how you appear in a social setting. Simpler and more direct than 'conversational labor.'
other_words.misses: Less precise about the performance element — someone with social anxiety experiences social fatigue too, and you were clear that is not what this is.

other_words.definition: The resistance or heaviness felt when maintaining a social connection that requires effort beyond what genuine interest would supply.
other_words.captures: The weight of continuing to engage when you do not actually want to. Emphasizes that the effort pulls on you.
other_words.misses: More poetic than precise; less commonly used than the others here.

output.plain_english: The specific tiredness that comes from performing interest in conversation you do not want to have — the exhaustion of keeping up the appearance of engagement when your actual interest is absent.
output.share_line: One word that comes close is 'conversational labor' — the deliberate effort of faking engagement. If you want something simpler, 'social fatigue' captures the tiredness without the anxiety.

cases.name: friend-good-news-dont-resolve-ambiguity

input.description: A friend told me their good news and I felt something drop before I felt happy for them. The happy part was real. So was the other part, and I don't have a word for it that isn't just 'jealous', which isn't quite right either.
input.context: They deserved it completely and I'd have been upset for them if it hadn't happened. It passed in about a minute. I still think about it.

cases.guards: The exact live bug report that produced 'compunction' as a strained primary match plus a string of invented specifics (the friend 'deserved' it stated as the tool's own conclusion rather than the visitor's, 'a flash of your own lack', 'authentic joy... took over'). PRIMARY MATCH RULE: best_match.word must fit the CENTRAL, ordinary meaning of the description — not an obscure/archaic sense that smuggles in an unstated element (guilt, wrongdoing, resentment). DON'T RESOLVE THE AMBIGUITY: nothing may declare the first feeling WAS or WASN'T envy/comparison/personal lack as a flat fact the model decided — the visitor's own uncertainty must survive into the answer (e.g. 'the description doesn't establish which'). Any claim that the visitor 'knew' something (like the friend deserving it) must trace to the visitor's OWN supplied context, not be invented — check it's grounded in the context field before treating it as a violation.

ingredients: An immediate physical drop or pang
Authentic happiness for your friend that followed
Uncertainty about what caused the first feeling
The feeling passing quickly
Knowing they deserved the good news
what_you_described.tension: Real joy for someone you care about, alongside a real but unnamed sensation that arrived first — both genuine, neither canceling the other out

best_match.definition: A sharp, sudden feeling of pain, sadness, or regret — often physical in its sensation, often brief
best_match.why_it_fits: You described something that dropped and passed in about a minute, with a physical quality to it. A pang names that sharp, sudden arrival without claiming to know what it means. It fits the sensation without diagnosing the cause.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: Pang usually implies a single clear source (regret, loss, hunger). Your description leaves the source uncertain — it could involve comparison, longing, disappointment, or something else entirely. Pang names the sensation itself, but doesn't resolve what prompted it.

other_words.definition: A sudden tightening or stopping sensation in the chest — often emotional rather than physical, often momentary
other_words.captures: The physical, almost involuntary quality of what arrived before your conscious happiness did. The sense that something happened to you rather than something you decided to feel.
other_words.misses: Less specific about whether the feeling involves comparison or lack; more purely about the bodily sensation itself

other_words.definition: A brief, bright moment of feeling or thought that arrives and passes before you can fully name it
other_words.captures: The speed and the incompleteness — you still don't have a word for it, and it was gone before you could examine it. Also the sense that you glimpsed something without fully understanding it.
other_words.misses: Even more indefinite than pang; trades precision about the sensation for precision about the timing. Useful if you want to honor that you genuinely didn't register what it was.

output.plain_english: An immediate sharp feeling in your body that dropped and passed within a minute, arriving before your genuine happiness for your friend registered. You're uncertain whether it involved comparing yourself to them, noticing something you wanted, disappointment in yourself, or something else entirely. It was real and physical, and it doesn't fit into 'jealous' because you wanted this for them and would have been upset if it hadn't happened.
output.share_line: One word that comes close is a pang — that sharp drop you felt, arriving fast and leaving fast. It names the sensation without claiming to know what caused it, which seems to match what you're describing: you felt something real, but its meaning is still unclear to you.

cases.name: meeting-mispronunciation-no-adequate-match

input.description: The specific discomfort of watching someone confidently mispronounce a word in a meeting and deciding in that half-second whether correcting them is worth the awkwardness it will cause everyone else in the room.

cases.guards: Tests the new NO ADEQUATE MATCH pathway end to end (PRIMARY MATCH RULE's 'prefer NO EXACT WORD over an impressive but semantically strained answer'). If match comes back NO ADEQUATE MATCH: best_match.word/language/pronunciation/definition should be empty rather than a coined phrase / meta-statement about the absence dressed up as a candidate ('No established single word', 'the discomfort of a no-win moment') — cleanNoMatchWord strips exactly that pattern server-side (check-golden can't see this by structure alone; eyeball it). where_it_doesnt becomes essential in this case and must say plainly what's missing. plain_english must stand on its own as the real answer. share_line must use the NO ADEQUATE MATCH framing ('There may not be one word for this...'). This case may instead legitimately come back CLOSE or PARTIAL MATCH with a real short phrase (e.g. 'caught between') — either outcome is fine as long as word/match/where_it_doesnt stay internally consistent.

ingredients: A moment of recognition (someone said something wrong)
Split-second mental calculation of consequences
Awareness of multiple conflicting interests (correctness vs. social comfort)
Discomfort suspended in indecision
what_you_described.tension: Knowing the right thing to do (correct them) and the costly thing to do (let it go) are in direct conflict, and you have almost no time to choose between them.

best_match.definition: The discomfort or hesitation that arises from an action that would create awkwardness or tension in a social setting, even when the action itself is justified.
best_match.why_it_fits: It names the specific discomfort you feel — not embarrassment for them, not guilt about staying silent, but the friction itself: the sense that speaking up will cost everyone present, and you're calculating whether it's worth paying. It captures the half-second pause, the awareness of consequences radiating outward.
best_match.where_it_doesnt: Social friction is slightly more general than your moment — it could describe the friction before any number of socially costly truths. Your description is more specific: the friction of a correction in particular, where you're weighing one person's error against everyone else's comfort.

other_words.definition: The judicious management of what one says and when, balancing honesty against harmony.
other_words.captures: The deliberation itself — the split-second weighing of whether this moment requires you to prioritize accuracy or group ease.
other_words.misses: Tact is about a choice you make. Your description is about the discomfort of being caught between two choices that both have a cost.

other_words.definition: Acute embarrassment or chagrin; historically, self-inflicted discomfort as a spiritual discipline.
other_words.captures: The visceral, immediate sting of being in an awkward position — the feeling-in-the-body of the moment.
other_words.misses: Mortification is usually about your own shame. Here you're not ashamed; you're uncomfortable about the awkwardness the correction would inflict on others.

output.plain_english: The uncomfortable pause before deciding whether to correct someone, when you're aware that speaking up will make the room uncomfortable even though silence costs something too.
output.share_line: One phrase that comes close is social friction — that specific discomfort of knowing an action is right but that it will cost everyone at the table.
